Moreover, the available studies varied in outcome measures (Table 3 ), resulting from different study designs (Table 4 ); for example, outcome measures such as sensitivity and specificity were reported inconsistently. Additionally, many of the studies had small sample sizes, which further hinders direct comparison (Tables 3 and 4 ). Results From a total of 945 records identified in the databases over the past 25 years, 19 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed (Fig. 1 ). The results regarding the relationship between IRT and joint US are presented in Table 3 and are further explained in the text below. Eight of the 19 included studies reported sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the curve (AUC) derived from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. These findings are summarized in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Graphical representation of a sensitivity, b specificity, and c area under the curve (AUC) derived from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. Studies reporting sensitivity and specificity values were included. Values are shown exemplarily for Tmax. Several studies did not use a simple Tmax parameter but instead applied alternative metrics, which are also presented here: Morales-Ivorra et al. used the ThermoJIS, Tan et al. (2024, 2025) applied a composite score, Triantafyllias et al. used HRR, and Vasdev et al. reported the knee–thigh differential. No 95% confidence intervals were reported for sensitivity and specificity in the mentioned studies. For the area under the curve (AUC), 95% confidence intervals were reported in the majority of studies; however, two studies provided only a single AUC value, for which no 95% confidence intervals are shown The diseases investigated include RA, PsA, Juvenile Idiopathic arthritis (JIA), SpA, gout, osteoarthritis (OA), see Table 4 for comparison. The majority of the studies focused on patients with RA ( n = 13) or mixed disease cohorts ( n = 4). Two studies included patients with other inflammatory arthritis associated diseases (juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), n = 1 and PsA, n = 1). Only one study investigated patients under 18 years of age, while all others focused on adults (further information to study populations in Table 4 ). The sample sizes of the studies ranged from small pilot cohorts to larger datasets. In all included studies, joint US served as the reference standard (see Table 5 for comparison of methodology). No studies comparing IRT with MRI and bone scintigraphy were identified in the systematic search. While methods were used in these studies varied (see Table 5 ), most of them employed standardized room conditions, acclimatization phases, and manual region-of-interest (ROI) selection, whereas some applied algorithm-based segmentation. Subtle but potentially significant differences exist in the processing of temperature parameters, contributing to heterogeneity in the literature. For example, Tan et al. used composite scores to assess inflammatory activity across multiple joints [ 89 , 96 ]; Triantafyllias et al. developed a new thermographic parameter during hotspot identification [ 79 ]. Morales-Ivorra [ 78 ] and Umapathy et al. [ 97 ] process raw data using machine learning and advanced algorithms to evaluate inflammatory activity (further information to study populations in Table 5 ). The risk of bias was assessed using the QUADAS-2 assessment tool as recommended by the PRISMA guidelines [ 80 , 81 ], see Table 6 . This revealed potential sources of bias, for example, due to small cohort sizes [ 83 , 84 ] or the exclusion of significant comorbidities (e.g., osteoarthritis [ 79 ]). None of the identified studies used a predefined cut-off, which carries the risk of overestimating test performance. Overview of the included studies Studies focusing on knee joints The following section summarizes the results of studies evaluating IRT and joint US in the assessment of knee arthritis, with particular emphasis on their diagnostic potential and accuracy. Ahn et al. studied 30 patients with swollen knees who were scheduled for arthrocentesis at a tertiary hospital [ 82 ]. All patients had knee effusion and a variety of diagnoses, including RA, SpA, OA, and other conditions. The patients underwent IRT, joint US, and arthrocentesis. Power Doppler (PD)-positive joints, which are indicative of hypervascularization and synovitis, exhibited significantly higher values across all temperature parameters (all; p < 0.05), e.g. Tavg 32.1 °C vs 29.1 °C. White blood cell counts correlated with PD positivity ( p = 0.010)), though no association was observed with thermographic parameters. ROC curve analysis indicated demonstrated good diagnostic performance of Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg for identifying PD positivity (AUC 0.764–0.790). For instance, Tavg demonstrated a sensitivity of 87.5% and a specificity of 68.5% at a cut-off of 30.1 °C (AUC = 0.770, 95% CI 0.581–0.959) [ 82 ]. In a subsequent study focusing on knee joints in arthritis, Vasdev et al. compared 50 patients with RA to 50 age- and sex-matched healthy controls recruited from hospital staff [ 98 ]. In contrast to the previous protocol, IRT images were obtained from the lateral aspect of the knee with the joint positioned at 90° flexion. To establish a control, a circle of equal radius was positioned on the lateral mid-thigh. Tavg values were measured for each ROI, and a knee–thigh differential (Tavg knee – Tavg thigh) was calculated [ 98 ]. Tavg was higher in RA patients than in in the control group (32.7  °C (95% CI 32.37–33.0) vs 31.5  °C (95% CI 31.24–31.74), p < 0.05). A significant difference in knee–thigh differential was observed (1.08  °C (95% CI 0.91–1.99) vs − 0.52  °C (95% CI − 0.66 to − 0.37), p < 0.05), but no significant association with PD grade was found [ 98 ]. ROC analysis showed an AUC of 0.998 ( p = 0.001), with sensitivity 100% (95% CI 92.5–100%) and specificity 94.4% (95% CI 84.3–98.8%). Notably, 86% of patients were classified as PD grade II, indicating relatively high disease activity [ 98 ]. IRT and US of the knee joints were also evaluated in the work of Umapathy et al., including 30 RA patients and 30 healthy controls [ 97 ]. IRT data were automatically segmented using the RIBS (Regional Isotherm-Based Segmentation) algorithm to detect hotspots within the ROI on grey-scale images. Temperature parameters and statistical features (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) were extracted from the segmented images and compared between RA patients and controls [ 97 ]. IRT revealed significant differences between RA patients and controls in extracted parameters and skin temperature (all p -values < 0.01). Temperature parameters demonstrated a strong correlation between biochemical markers (ESR: erythrocyte sedimentation rate, CRP: C-reactive protein) and clinical scores (DAS28: disease activity score 28, HAQ: health assessment questionnaire). The correlation was significant at the p < 0.01 level. The presence of synovitis, as indicated by GS- (effusion) and PD-positivity (perfusion, color fraction), also demonstrated a correlation with CRP, ESR, DAS28, and HAQ. A direct comparison between IRT and joint US was not performed [ 97 ]. Tan et al. investigated 190 knees from 95 patients with rheumatoid arthritis to assess the correlation between thermographic parameters (Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg) and ultrasound findings of knee arthritis [ 95 ]. Higher Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg values were significantly associated with joint inflammation detected by grayscale (GS) and power Doppler (PD) ultrasound (GS: correlation coefficients ranged from 0.27 to 0.49, p < 0.01; PD: correlation coefficients ranged from 0.21 to 0.43, p < 0.05). In addition, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg in identifying a PD score > 0 ranged from 0.63 to 0.82 [ 95 ]. In summary, findings for the knee joint indicate that PD-positive joints were associated with elevated temperature parameters, even though grading of inflammation was not feasible [ 82 , 95 ]. Moreover, the use of thermal imaging has proven effective in distinguishing RA-affected knees from those of healthy individuals [ 98 ]. Automatic segmentation of IRT further offers a practical approach, producing results comparable to joint US [ 97 ]. Wrist and finger joints Lerkvaleekul et al. compared IRT and joint US findings of the wrist in 46 patients with JIA and 15 healthy controls [ 86 ]. JIA patients were categorized as having inactive or active arthritis. The latter category was further subdivided into mild and moderate-to-severe disease based on physical examination. Both Tmax and Tavg in the ROI were found to be significantly higher in the active arthritis group compared to the inactive patients and controls (for example Tavg: Healthy controls 30.27 °C ± SD 0.67; Arthritis 31.37 ± SD 1.49, p < 0.05). In subgroup analyses, Tavg and Tmax were highest in the moderate-to-severe group, differing significantly from all other groups, including mild arthritis ( p < 0.05) [ 86 ]. No significant differences were found between mild arthritis and inactive disease. ROC curve analysis was performed to define a cut-off between healthy controls and the moderate-to-severe arthritis group. For instance, the AUC was 0.93 Tavg > 31 °C (sensitivity 85.7%, specificity 80.0%). For the joint US, the AUC was 0.87, with a sensitivity of 83.3% and specificity of 81.3%. Due to the limited sample size, correlation analysis between thermal imaging and joint US could not be performed; yet the results seemed comparable [ 86 ]. Subsequently, Tan et al. studied 70 wrist joints in RA patients to investigate how IRT and US findings relate to clinical signs of arthritis [ 90 ]. Wrists were categorized into four clinical groups: (1) swollen and tender (S1T1), (2) swollen and non-tender (S1T0), (3) non-swollen and tender (S0T1), and (4) non-swollen and non-tender (S0T0). Both swollen-joint groups demonstrated higher thermographic parameters compared to the non-swollen/non-tender group (all p < 0.05). There were no observed differences between the non-swollen/tender and non-swollen/non-tender groups. Similar results were observed for joint US ( p < 0.05). The authors highlighted the high comparability between the two diagnostic techniques; however, explicit correlations between IRT and joint US were not analyzed, though the overall findings were considered similar [ 90 ]. The same group also focused on the examination of finger joints. In one study, they evaluated 37 RA patients with at least one swollen or tender joint, documented in a binary manner (tenderness/swelling present = 1, absent = 0) [ 88 ]. ROIs were manually placed over the MCPs, PIPs, and wrists. Thermographic parameters (Tmax, Tmin, Tavg, Tmax − min) were significantly higher in PD-positive joints (PD-score > 0) than in PD-negative joints (PD-score = 0) (all p < 0.001). Similar significant differences were observed for Grey-scale findings (all p < 0.001). No significant associations were found between thermographic parameters and clinical features such as tenderness or swelling. The study did not report sensitivity and specificity [ 88 ]. In a separate study, Tan et al. investigated subclinical inflammation in the MCP joints of 42 asymptomatic RA patients, comparing joint US and IRT [ 92 ]. Joints with active subclinical synovitis (PD-score > 1 or GS-score > 2) showed significantly higher thermographic parameters (Tmin, Tavg, Tmax; p = 0.002–0.003; Pearson’s r = 0.447–0.465) [ 92 ]. Furthermore, the research group expanded its studies to include the detection of subclinical disease activity. They examined the right wrists of 87 RA patients, categorizing them into asymptomatic and symptomatic groups (tender and/or swollen) [ 91 ]. Significant differences were found for all thermographic parameters between symptomatic and asymptomatic groups, for example, Tavg 32.0 ± 1.6 vs. 31.0 ± 1.5 ( p = 0.006). GS and PD scores were higher in symptomatic wrists compared to asymptomatic wrists. Among asymptomatic wrists, those with abnormalities in joint US showed elevated thermographic parameters compared to those without abnormalities, e.g., Tavg 31.5 ± 1.2 vs. 30.3 ± 1.7 ( p = 0.007) [ 91 ]. These results further support the utility of IRT in detecting subclinical synovitis. In another study, Tan et al. investigated whether summed thermographic parameters (Tmax, Tmin, Tavg) could be used to predict sonographic abnormalities of the bilateral metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints [ 96 ]. To this end, all five MCP joints were examined bilaterally in 81 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and thermographic parameters were assessed for each joint and additionally summed across joints. They found that higher summed Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg values were significantly correlated with joint inflammation detected by GS and PD US (GS: correlation coefficients ranged from 0.27 to 0.49, p < 0.05; PD: correlation coefficients ranged from 0.45 to 0.52, p < 0.05). Furthermore, ROC-curve analysis of summed thermographic temperature values for the prediction of a summed PD score ≥ 1 across bilateral MCP joints yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) ranging from 0.80 to 0.82[ 96 ]. Tan et al. also developed a composite Total Temperature Score to detect subclinical synovitis. They assessed subclinical disease activity in 80 RA patients using IRT and joint US [ 93 ]. Patients were stratified by DAS28 into remission/low disease activity (< 3.2) and moderate-to-high disease activity (> 3.2). US examinations included the MCP, PIP, wrist, elbow, and knee joints. The joints most frequently showing PD positivity were the wrists (62.7%), followed by the second MCPs (37.0%), third MCPs (33.8%), fourth MCPs (24.8%), and fifth MCPs (20.9%) (all p < 0.05). In these joints, higher composite Total temperature scores were associated with PD-positivity scores (all; p < 0.05). ROC curve analysis established cut-off values for total IRT parameters, with Total Tmax achieving a sensitivity of 95.7% and a specificity of 54.5% for identifying PD-positive joints [ 93 ]. A different strategy for detecting synovitis was employed by Morales et al. They developed a machine learning–based Thermographic Joint Inflammation Score (ThermoJIS) to detect arthritis [ 78 ]. The study included a large development cohort of 449 participants (development set), comprising patients with RA, PsA, undifferentiated arthritis, OA, and healthy controls. For all patients with rheumatologic diseases, joint US of both hands (wrists, MCPs, and PIPs) was used as the reference standard, with GS and PD abnormalities combined into sum scores. Thermographic images were acquired under non-standardized conditions, intentionally reflecting real-world data. ROIs were automatically defined by an algorithm detecting major intensity variations in the images, and their thermal features were linked to the PD sum score to evaluate associations with synovitis. Data from this development set were used for training and tuning of the machine learning model. Using these data, ThermoJIS was generated [ 78 ]. In a validation cohort of 146 RA patients, ThermoJIS was tested for detecting active synovitis, with joint US again serving as the gold standard. ThermoJIS showed moderate correlations with grey-scale synovial hypertrophy ( r = 0.49, p < 0.001) and Power Doppler ( r = 0.51, p < 0.001). Sensitivity was 91% and specificity was 51%. Importantly, ThermoJIS also detected subclinical activity in RA patients in remission (DAS28-CRP < 2.6). To enhance specificity, the authors proposed classifying a range of scores as “indeterminate,” which adjusted sensitivity and specificity to 87% and 82%, respectively. However, 43% of the validation cohort fell into this indeterminate range, which the authors noted could limit the practical utility of the method [ 78 ]. Interestingly, in a subsequent study on the same validation cohort, the authors combined ThermoJIS with the patient’s global assessment (PGA), creating ThermoDAI, or with PGA and CRP, creating ThermoDAI-CRP [ 87 ]. Both indices demonstrated stronger correlations with active synovitis detected by joint ultrasound than ThermoJIS alone (e.g., Spearman’s r : ThermoDAI-CRP vs. PD sum score = 0.61; ThermoJIS vs. PD sum score = 0.51) [ 87 ]. ThermoDAI and ThermoDAI-CRP also correlated strongly with established disease activity scores (CDAI, SDAI, DAS28-CRP) and showed comparable sensitivity and specificity for detecting active synovitis [ 87 ]. Tan et al. also investigated the relationship between disease activity (operationalized using DAS28) in 37 RA patients with composite IRT and US scores [ 89 ]. For the IRT, they determined the lowest measured temperature of a patient’s joint and then calculated the difference between Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg for each joint examined. The differences for each joint were then added together to form the composite scores MAX, MIN, and AVG. They also formed composite scores for the US (total PD and total GS). In addition, combined scores were also formed from the results of the IRT and US (MAX (PD), MIN (PD), and AVG (PD)). The statistical correlation with DAS28 was then examined [ 89 ]. This showed that both the combined scores MAX (PD) and AVG (PD) correlated significantly with the DAS28 (for example Pearson correlation coefficient MAX (PD) (95% CI), 0.393 (0.079, 0.636), P = 0.016). IRT and US alone did not achieve a significant correlation. This indicates the value of using both diagnostic methods in parallel [ 89 ]. In previous studies, cutaneous surface temperature was typically measured once and compared with joint US. Capo et al. (2015) employed a different approach, comparing 10 patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and 11 healthy controls [ 83 ]. ROIs were manually defined on the dominant hand (MCP, PIP, DIP), and a thermographic baseline was established. Standardized isometric contractions of the dominant hand muscles were then performed using a dynamometer, with various temperature parameters recorded over 5 min. PsA patients exhibited significantly higher temperature values ( p < 0.0025) and faster temperature fluctuations compared to controls [ 83 ]. Some temperature parameters correlated with PD-defined disease activity. However, the small sample size (6 with active and 4 with inactive disease) limited the subgroup analysis, allowing only qualitative conclusions [ 83 ]. In a subsequent methodological study, Capo et al. (2018) compared 10 RA patients with 11 healthy controls [ 84 ]. In contrast to the findings of the 2015 PsA study, RA patients demonstrated lower dynamic temperature values compared to the control group. A joint US was also performed on RA patients to facilitate a comparison with the findings from IRT. Due to the limited sample size, only qualitative conclusions could be drawn, and no further details were provided [ 84 ]. Overall, when comparing the ability of IRT and US to detect arthritis in wrist joints, both modalities demonstrated similar performance in head-to-head ROC analyses [ 86 ]. IRT successfully identified both symptomatic and asymptomatic inflamed wrist joints, with inflammation defined by ultrasound criteria [ 90 , 91 ]. Similar findings were reported for asymptomatic MCP joints [ 92 ]. Moreover, the application of automated image analysis techniques has shown promising results, as demonstrated by Morales-Ivorra et al. [ 78 , 87 ], while Capo et al. highlighted the potential of dynamic thermal measurements as a valuable complementary approach [ 83 , 84 ]. The combination of IRT and US could measure disease activity even more accurately than either method alone [ 89 ]. Other ioints (e.g., elbow, foot) and mixed disease spectra Studies assessing the diagnostic performance of thermography for the other joints, such as the elbow or the foot joints, and mixed disease spectra are limited. Tan et al. evaluated elbow IRT in 30 RA patients, performing bilateral examinations [ 94 ]. ROIs were manually selected from all four sides of the elbow joints, and Tmax, Tmin, and Tavg were measured. The composite scores were generated by summing Tmax values from all four aspects to create a total Tmax score (MAX). The same procedure was applied for Tmin and Tavg (MIN and AVG). GS- and PD- subscores were also summed. A notable correlation was identified between the composite thermographic scores and PD scores in both elbows. For instance, the correlation coefficient (95% CI) for MAX was 0.47 (0.12–0.70). Thermographic scores and grey-scale findings have been found to correlate only with the right elbow ( p < 0.05) [ 94 ]. Moreover, Gizinska et al. examined the dorsal feet of 81 RA patients with pain and stiffness, compared to 39 healthy controls [ 85 ]. RA patients exhibited significantly higher mean ROI temperatures than controls ( p < 0.05). However, ultrasound-detected inflammation generally did not correspond with elevated temperature parameters, except in the right MTP1 (metatarsophalangeal joint), left MTP2, and two ROIs (right ROI 1, left ROI 2), where p < 0.05 [ 85 ]. Triantafyllias et al. assessed multiple joints in 75 patients with mixed disease spectra, including RA, PsA, SpA, and gout, as well as 70 healthy controls [ 79 ]. A novel parameter, the hotspot/ROI ratio (HRR), was defined using a k-means clustering algorithm and compared with PD grades I–III. Fingers, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles were examined, with analyses conducted both for the overall patient group and for disease-specific subgroups. Tmin/max/avg were significantly higher in PD-positive joints compared to controls. HRR showed the same pattern ( p < 0.0001) and, together with Tavg, distinguished PD-positive from PD-negative joints (HRR: 0.313 ± 0.031 vs 0.103 ± 0.027, p < 0.0001; Tavg: 31.43 ± 0.32 vs 30.88 ± 0.31, p = 0.026). HRR correlated moreover with semi-quantitative PD scores, except between PDUS grade I and II ( p = 0.417). ROC analysis of HRR yielded an AUC of 0.76 (95% CI 0.70–0.82) with 79% sensitivity and 65% specificity. The best performance was seen at the wrist (AUC 0.91, 95% CI 0.84–0.98; sensitivity 83%, specificity 88%) and large joints (AUC 0.87, 95% CI 0.80–0.94; sensitivity 82%, specificity 79%) [ 79 ]. The elbow and foot regions have been investigated to a limited extent. While studies on the elbow emphasize the potential diagnostic value of IRT [ 94 ], investigations of the feet using the applied methodology have shown little clinical benefit [ 85 ]. Further research, potentially with modified study designs, appears necessary. Notably, Triantafyllias et al. demonstrated the strong diagnostic performance of IRT [ 79 ]; using HRR-based processing of temperature parameters, they were able to identify associations with ultrasound-derived inflammation grades [ 79 ]. Nevertheless, studies involving larger cohorts and more diverse disease populations remain scarce [ 78 , 79 ]. Discussion This systematic review summarizes the evidence on medical IRT in rheumatology, focusing on studies that used joint US as an established reference [ 100 , 101 , 111 ]or evaluated both modalities concurrently. To our knowledge, it is the first systematic review to directly compare IRT with an established diagnostic modality and among the few works assessing the diagnostic value of IRT in rheumatology practice in general [ 41 , 71 ]. The reported studies suggest that IRT can distinguish healthy joints from arthritic joints, with results generally consistent with US [ 79 , 86 , 98 ]. Additionally, like joint US, IRT appears capable of detecting both active and inactive disease [ 79 , 93 ]. The current literature on IRT and its relationship to joint US is highly heterogeneous regarding preparation of the patient and data processing following data acquisition (see Table 5 ). While most studies applied standardized preparation protocols, still differences in factors such as room temperature, acclimatization time, camera placement, and especially ROI selection limit the comparability of results [ 112 ]. The use of international guidelines, such as those from the European Association of Thermology [ 102 , 103 ], and standardized approaches like the Glamorgan Protocol for ROI selection [ 104 ], may contribute to enhancing consistency across studies. In two studies, these guidelines had already been implemented [ 79 , 85 ]. As described before, the methods used to evaluate thermographic images vary significantly across studies. Some studies employed relatively straightforward metrics, such as the average temperature of an ROI [ 82 ] or its ratio to the average temperature of an independent skin area [ 98 ]. Another approach was the use of composite score of multiple joints [ 89 ]. Others applied even more sophisticated approaches, including automatic ROI selection with machine learning [ 78 ] or the hotspot-to-ROI ratio (HRR), which identifies ‘hotspots’ in the ROI via clustering and correlates strongly with joint US results [ 79 ]. Several studies had small sample sizes (20–27 subjects) [ 83 , 84 ], limiting the strength of their conclusions. The majority of the research focused on RA (13 of 19 studies), with only four studies including mixed patient groups. In some cases, important differential diagnoses such as osteoarthritis were excluded [ 79 ], despite its high prevalence, impact on disability, and association with increased joint temperature [ 113 , 114 ]. The aforementioned limitations and methodological differences may contribute to the wide reported range of sensitivity and specificity (sensitivity for detecting arthritis ranged from 79 to 100%, specificity from 51–94%, as depicted in Fig. 2 ). This broad range underscores the need for further standardization [ 41 , 71 ]. Findings of good specificity such as those by Triantafyllias et al. demonstrate the potential utility in routine clinical practice [ 79 ]. On the other hand, the methodological heterogeneity in IRT has also led to the development of multiple approaches that could enhance its diagnostic application. Some methods, such as machine learning–based approaches [ 78 ] or cumulative temperature scores [ 93 ], show high sensitivity for detecting disease activity. Others, such as the HRR parameter demonstrated high specificity [ 79 ]. Combining these approaches in a stepwise diagnostic framework could be valuable in different clinical scenarios [ 89 ]. Additionally, dynamic test procedures, as used by Capo et al. [ 83 , 84 ], may complement static assessments in cases with inconclusive findings in the future. Integrating IRT with joint US has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Given the limitations of joint US, including high examiner dependency and personnel intensity [ 50 ], thermography offers a valuable complement, by enabling rapid, examiner-independent assessment of multiple joints, potentially even by non-medical personnel. Overall, thermography appears to be a promising adjunct for diagnosing and monitoring arthritis, providing high sensitivity and specificity depending on the method used. Its performance seems to be particularly strong in larger joints, such as the knee and wrist [ 79 , 98 ], while results in smaller joints, like the MCPs, are also encouraging [ 92 , 96 ]. Other small joints, such as those of the feet, showed disappointing results; however, this was observed in only a single study. Further research in this area is needed [ 85 ]. Several of the included studies were conducted by the same author group (Tan et al., see Table 3 ), reflecting the current structure of the research field. While studies were identified through a predefined, comprehensive search strategy independent of authorship, this concentration may limit the independence and generalizability of the evidence and should be considered when interpreting the findings. To minimize risk of bias in future studies, it also appears important to test predefined cut-offs in as realistic and diverse study populations as possible, encompassing a variety of disease conditions, in order to better estimate performance in routine clinical practice. In the future research is needed to assess the applicability of thermography in outpatient settings for both diagnosis and follow-up, and to evaluate its reliability in supporting treatment decisions compared with joint US. Looking forward, this approach could complement telemedicine-based assessments [ 72 ] and may provide a valuable tool to support AI-assisted patient care within automated diagnostic or therapeutic workflows, potentially enhancing both efficiency and the accuracy of clinical decision-making [ 74 , 75 ]. Moreover, its utility in conditions other than RA and in paediatric populations warrants further investigation. documents.title: Clinical efficacy and radiological changes of proximal fibular osteotomy for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to analyze the clinical efficacy, safety, and radiological changes of proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO) for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis (MKOA).
METHODS: Since the establishment of the databases, we searched all studies involving proximal fibular osteotomy in PubMed, Proquest, Scopus, and Web of Science. The outcomes of interest were visual analog scale (VAS), knee function scores, radiological results, and complication rates. Case-control studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale, and randomized controlled trials were independently evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration's assessment tool. Heterogeneity was tested using I², and a fixed or random-effects model was selected for meta-analysis based on the heterogeneity results. Of the 21 studies included, 17 were case-control studies and 4 were RCTs.
RESULTS: A total of 21 studies, including 1006 knees, were included in the meta-analysis. PFO can effectively alleviate the most troubling pain for patients (VAS: mean difference MD = -4.25 [-5.51; -3.00]) and significantly improve postoperative knee function (Hedges' g = 2.41 [1.35-3.47]). Moreover, due to the minimal surgical trauma, the incidence of postoperative complications is low, with sensory abnormalities of the common peroneal nerve being the most common adverse event (5.93%; 95% CI: 2.15-11.25%), followed by common peroneal nerve palsy (2.25%; 95% CI: 0.14-6.14%), fracture (0.56%; 95% CI: 0-1.74%), and only two cases of infection were reported in all included studies, both of which recovered within half a year. In addition, PFO can effectively improve the radiological outcomes, with an increase in HKA (MD = 1.73 [0.33; 3.13]), a decrease in FTA (MD = -3.83 [-4.05; -3.62]), an increase in knee joint space (MD = 2.66 mm[2.38; 2.94]), and an increase in the ratio of medial to lateral knee joint space (MD = 0.16 [0.15; 0.18]).
CONCLUSION: In the field of MKOA treatment, PFO has shown a promising prospect. The clinical function scores and radiological assessments improved after PFO in this meta-analysis, indicating that this surgical method can significantly improve patients' symptoms, correct the varus deformity of the lower limb alignment, and is safe. However, it must be pointed out that the quality of evidence supporting this conclusion is still low, and radiological studies are relatively few. Therefore, future studies need to be conducted in more diverse patient populations, incorporating more radiological indicators and providing higher-quality clinical evidence.

Epidemiological studies have shown that about 50% of individuals over the age of 60 are affected by knee osteoarthritis, and this proportion rises to as high as 80% in those over 70 years old. When conservative treatment is no longer effective for MKOA symptoms, surgical treatment can be considered [ 3 , 4 ].Over the past few decades, total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) have been the main methods for treating late-stage knee osteoarthritis [ 5 , 6 ]. However, these methods have limitations such as significant surgical trauma, long postoperative recovery time, and potential complications like prosthesis loosening or infection. Moreover, the indications for TKA and UKA are relatively strict, and they may not be the best choices for patients with early-stage knee osteoarthritis or those with poor knee alignment. In recent years, with the in-depth study of knee biomechanics, proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO) has gradually been applied to the treatment of MKOA as a minimally invasive surgical method. PFO is based on the uneven settlement theory, which changes the load distribution of the knee joint to reduce the pressure on the medial compartment of the knee, thereby alleviating pain and improving knee function [ 7 ]. However, there is still controversy regarding the efficacy and safety of PFO. Some studies have shown that PFO can significantly improve lower limb alignment and medial joint space narrowing, while others have pointed out that its effects may vary among individuals [ 8 ]. Additionally, the long-term radiological changes and potential complications after PFO surgery also need further exploration [ 9 – 11 ]. So far, only a few meta-analyses have been conducted on the clinical outcomes after PFO surgery. Due to the limited number of studies or outcomes included, especially the insufficient analysis of the radiological outcomes after PFO in these analyses. This study includes an analysis of HKA, FTA, and the ratio of medial to lateral joint space, with a total of 15 articles included in the radiological outcomes, more comprehensively evaluating the changes in lower limb alignment after PFO. The purpose of this study is to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis, summarizing the clinical efficacy, radiological outcomes, and complications of PFO in the treatment of knee joint diseases, in order to provide evidence support for clinicians regarding the reasonable application of PFO in the treatment of knee joint diseases. Materials and methods We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to report the current systematic review and meta-analysis. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews, with the registration number CRD420251026547. Literature search Two authors conducted a structured search of the electronic databases PubMed, Scopus, Proquest, and Web Of Science in April 2025, with no language restrictions other than English. The search covered all publications from the inception of the databases to April 2025. All extracted data were systematically collected and sorted using an electronic spreadsheet. We used the following search string: ((proximal fibular osteotomy[Title/Abstract]) OR (high fibular osteotomy[Title/Abstract])) AND (((((Knee Osteoarthritides[Title/Abstract]) OR (Knee Osteoarthritis[Title/Abstract])) OR (Osteoarthritis of Knee[Title/Abstract])) OR (Osteoarthritis of the Knee[Title/Abstract])) OR ((((Knee Osteoarthritides[MeSH]) OR (Knee Osteoarthritis[MeSH])) OR (Osteoarthritis of Knee[MeSH])) OR (Osteoarthritis of the Knee[MeSH]))). Eligibility criteria We included original research articles, clinical trials, and cohort studies aimed at summarizing the objective and subjective clinical efficacy and radiological outcomes of PFO. Additionally, studies combining PFO with other surgeries, such as arthroscopic knee surgery, were excluded. We also searched the reference lists of relevant articles to minimize information loss. Inclusion criteria (1) Population: Patients with medial compartment knee osteoarthritis (MKOA), with or without other knee injuries; (2) Intervention: Studies focusing on proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO) as the sole surgical intervention for MKOA; (3) Comparator: Studies including patients not undergoing PFO or undergoing other non-PFO-related surgeries for MKOA; (4) Outcomes: Studies reporting at least one of the following outcomes: pain scores (e.g., VAS), knee function scores (e.g., OKS, KSS), radiological measurements (e.g., HKA, FTA), and complication rates; (5) Study Design: Original research articles, clinical trials, and cohort studies with a minimum follow-up of 7 months. Exclusion criteria (1) Studies combining PFO with other surgeries such as arthroscopic knee surgery; (2) Cadaveric, animal, and laboratory studies; (3) Studies with incomplete data or insufficient reporting of outcomes. Data extraction An electronic spreadsheet was used to extract sample size, subgroup variables, and the outcomes of knee pain and function after PFO (i.e., Visual Analog Score (VAS), Oxford Knee Score (OKS) [ 13 ], Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Hospital for Special Surgery Knee Score (HSS) [ 14 ], Knee Society Score (KSS), Japanese Orthopaedic Association Score (JOA), American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society Score (AOFAS), Short Form 12 (SF12), Range of Motion (ROM), Hip-Knee-Ankle Angle (HKA) reflecting lower limb alignment, Femoral-Tibial Angle (FTA), and the ratio of medial to lateral joint space and medial joint space size reflecting joint space relief). When discrepancies arose between the two reviewers during study selection or data extraction, a third reviewer was consulted to independently assess the disputed items.Regular cross-verification sessions and quality control meetings were held to ensure the accuracy and consistency of data extraction. Study selection Based on the search strategy, 1001 studies were identified from the databases, of which 21 reference articles met the inclusion criteria. The study selection process is outlined in Fig. 1 . Briefly, after removing duplicates and excluding studies that did not meet the eligibility criteria based on titles and abstracts, the full texts of the remaining studies were reviewed to determine final inclusion. Handling of mixed intervention studies Studies combining PFO with other surgical interventions were excluded if the individual effect of PFO could not be distinguished from the combined intervention. For studies reporting outcomes of both PFO alone and PFO combined with other surgeries, only the data pertaining to PFO alone were extracted and analyzed. The quality of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias(RoB) Assessment Tool [ 15 ], as shown in Figs. 2 and 3 . Green, yellow, and red represent low, unknown, and high risk, respectively. The Cochrane RoB tool was used to evaluate seven domains: selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, reporting bias, and other biases. Case-control studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ 16 ], with scores of 0–3 indicating low quality, 4–6 indicating moderate quality, and 7–9 indicating high quality. the NOS was used to evaluate three aspects: selection of study groups, comparability of groups, and assessment of outcomes. Studies with high risk of bias were excluded from sensitivity analyses to assess the impact on the stability of the results. The graph uses green for low risk, yellow for unclear risk, and red for high risk Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using the meta-analysis package in R software (version 8.0–2). Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and I². We considered P < 0.1 or I² > 50% to indicate significant heterogeneity, as these thresholds are widely accepted in meta-analysis to distinguish between substantial and low heterogeneity. If heterogeneity remained after sensitivity analysis, a random-effects model was used for the meta-analysis. P > 0.1 and I² < 50% indicated no heterogeneity, and the studies were assessed using a fixed-effects model. Continuous variables were described using mean differences (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), while binary data were described using odds ratios (OR) and 95% CI. Since various scoring methods were used to assess knee function outcomes in the included studies, we presented the effect sizes of outcomes such as Hedges’ g and 95% CI. For studies using the WOMAC score, we multiplied the knee function outcomes by -1 to align with the direction of improvement seen in other scoring systems. This transformation was necessary because lower WOMAC scores indicate better outcomes, unlike most other scores where higher values reflect better function. The transformation ensures that all effect sizes are interpreted consistently, with positive values indicating improvement. We investigated publication bias for outcomes involving 10 or more studies using funnel plots and Egger’s test, with all results presented using forest plots. Both methods were conducted using the meta-analysis package in R software, with the same version as above. Standardization of radiological measurements To reduce heterogeneity, we explicitly defined the radiological parameter measurement standards. as follows: (1) HKA is measured on full-length weight-bearing anteroposterior X-rays, as the angle formed by the centers of the femoral head, knee joint, and ankle joint. (2) FTA is also measured on full-length weight-bearing anteroposterior X-rays, defined as the lateral angle between the femoral and tibial mechanical axes. (3) Medial joint space width (mJSW) is measured at the narrowest point of the medial compartment on weight-bearing knee X-rays. (4) Medial-lateral joint space ratio is calculated by dividing the mJSW by the lateral JSW at the midpoints of each compartment. Studies deviating from these standards (e.g., non-weight-bearing images or alternative measurement landmarks) were flagged and assessed via sensitivity analysis. If they distorted results or significantly increased heterogeneity, they were excluded. Study selection A total of 21 papers, including 1006 knees, were included. The average number of knees examined in all studies was 48 (range: 11–203). The gender ratio was reported in 17 studies (Table 1 ). The average number of male participants was 9, and the average number of female patients was 38. The average age was reported in 19 papers as 61.07 ± 7.81 years (range: 13.4–67.1 years). The average BMI was reported as 26.77 ± 1.29 (range: 24.48–28.4); however, only 7 papers (40.3%) reported this. The study by Atlıhan [ 31 ] reported BMI separately for males and females. The KL grade was reported in 11 studies preoperatively, with 108 cases (10.7%) having KL ≥ 4. The average follow-up time was reported in 10 studies as 24.6 months. Two studies were excluded due to missing standard deviations. Given the high heterogeneity (I² = 98.7%, P < 0.1), a sensitivity analysis was performed. However, the sensitivity analysis showed similar results after removing the heterogeneity. Therefore, the data were analyzed using a random-effects model. The results indicated that among the 357 knees included in the 6 studies, the postoperative VAS score improved by 4.25 [-5.51; -3.00] (Fig. 4 ). This indicates a clinically significant reduction in pain, as a decrease of 2 points or more on the VAS is generally considered to be the minimal clinically important difference for pain relief. Patients undergoing PFO may experience a shorter recovery time and may return to daily activities more quickly. In the 21 studies we conducted, researchers encouraged patients to ambulate fully weight-bearing within 1–3 days post-surgery when pain was tolerable. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses We observed substantial heterogeneity in metrics such as the VAS, femorotibial angle FTA, and HKA, which compromised the credibility of our findings. To address this, we conducted sensitivity analyses by excluding lower-quality studies, resulting in significantly reduced heterogeneity and demonstrating high sensitivity. These findings warrant caution when interpreting results and drawing conclusions. Additionally, we performed subgroup analyses stratified by preoperative osteoarthritis severity to further mitigate heterogeneity (Figs. 13 , 14 and 15 ). For studies lacking documented KL grading, we requested original data from corresponding authors. Unresponsive studies were categorized based on joint space width and other radiographic parameters. Our results demonstrated that severe preoperative KOA leads to diminished postoperative outcomes following PFO. The distribution of included studies on either side of the center line is not perfectly symmetrical, suggesting the possibility of publication bias Discussion Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a common degenerative joint disease that significantly impacts the quality of life of middle-aged and elderly individuals. Medial compartment knee osteoarthritis (MKOA) is particularly prevalent and often leads to varus deformity and severe pain. In recent years, knee-sparing surgeries have gained popularity in the treatment of KOA, especially for MKOA. Among them, the proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO), based on the uneven settlement theory, has become a minimally invasive surgical option. According to the current evidence, it has the potential to shift the load from the medial to the lateral compartment, thereby alleviating pain and improving knee function. However, its long-term effectiveness still needs to be confirmed in more high-quality studies [ 39 – 41 ]. The increasing popularity of PFO in recent years can be attributed to its relatively simple surgical procedure and minimal invasiveness compared to other treatments such as high tibial osteotomy (HTO), unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) [ 9 , 42 – 44 ]. This meta-analysis shows that PFO is associated with improved knee pain and force line correction, indicating potential biomechanical benefits of this surgical approach in the included studies. However, due to limitations in research methods, the long-term lasting effects of these effects are still uncertain. A prior meta-analysis reported similar results, primarily focusing on improved clinical function scores post-PFO with limited analysis of radiological outcomes [ 5 ]. To bridge this gap, we conducted a more comprehensive analysis of radiological parameters, including HKA, FTA, and the ratio of medial to lateral joint space. By incorporating 15 articles, we aimed to better understand the changes in lower limb alignment following PFO. Previous studies have largely focused on clinical scores and pain relief, often neglecting the radiological outcomes after PFO. Our meta-analysis revealed that PFO can significantly correct varus deformity, as evidenced by a decrease in FTA (MD = -3.83 [-4.05; -3.62]). This finding is consistent with the biomechanical principle that removing a segment of the fibula can rebalance the soft tissues and ligaments around the knee, reducing the load on the medial compartment. Additionally, PFO led to an increase in the medial knee joint space (MD = 2.66 mm[2.38; 2.94]) and an increase in the medial to lateral joint space ratio (MD = 0.16 [0.15; 0.18]), further supporting the effectiveness of this surgical approach. Future research should incorporate a broader range of radiological indicators to explore the comprehensive impact of PFO on knee biomechanics. For instance, Guo et al. [ 24 ] reported improvements in tibial inclination (TI) and tibial tuberosity (TT) after PFO, suggesting benefits beyond lower limb alignment. Deng et al. [ 25 ] found that patients with a curved proximal fibula had better functional and radiological outcomes, indicating that patient selection based on anatomical characteristics may enhance the efficacy of PFO. The underlying mechanism of PFO remains a topic of ongoing research. The predominant theory is based on uneven settlement, where the fibula provides support to the lateral tibial plateau, preventing significant settling of the lateral side and leading to varus deformity as the medial side settles more rapidly with age [ 46 ]. However, other theories have been proposed. For example, Huang et al. [ 19 ] suggested that the effects of PFO might be due to muscle competition between the biceps femoris and the fibula. Biomechanical studies have shown that patients with varus deformity and KOA have higher peak activity levels in the peroneus longus muscle and lower peak activity levels in the biceps femoris muscle compared to healthy individuals [ 45 ]. Xie et al. [ 48 ] attributed the immediate symptom relief after PFO to changes in the ground reaction vector (GRV) at the foot level, which reduces the knee adduction moment. However, this theory was challenged by Guo et al. [ 24 ], who found no proximal migration of the ankle or ankle varus alignment after PFO. Another theory involves the phenomenon of coronal tibiofemoral subluxation or dislocation, where the lateral femoral condyle slides medially, increasing the knee adduction moment (KAM) and exacerbating varus deformity [ 47 ]. The improvement in clinical outcomes after PFO is thought to be linked to beneficial changes in skeletal remodeling, muscles, and ligaments. Some researchers have explored the biomechanical changes of PFO. Nie et al. [ 19 ] used 3D gait analysis and lower limb musculoskeletal models to study the biomechanics of PFO. They found that preoperatively, KOA patients had lower gait efficiency and higher overall knee adduction moment(KAM)peaks compared to healthy controls. By six months post-PFO, patients’ gait patterns resembled those of healthy controls. The peak muscle activity of the operated side’s biceps femoris increased immediately and remained high at six months, while the peak activity of the longus fibularis decreased immediately and then gradually recovered. KAM, a key indicator of medial tibiofemoral compartment loading during walking, showed an average reduction of 11.1% in the operated side’s overall peak KAM postoperatively. Mo et al. [ 53 ] used 3D finite element analysis to show that PFO reduces stress on the medial tibial plateau and increases it on the lateral tibial plateau.Among the 21 studies included, eight reported complications related to PFO. The most common complications were dorsal foot sensory abnormalities and common peroneal nerve palsy, with all cases resolving within six months [ 6 , 17 , 20 , 26 , 32 , 34 , 35 ]. Only two cases of infection were reported, each in separate studies, and both resolved within six months. While the reported complication profile appears favorable in these studies, primarily consisting of transient neurological symptoms, the low overall reporting rate (8/21) and potential under-reporting inherent in retrospective designs necessitate caution. The findings suggest that PFO may be a relatively safe procedure in experienced hands and within the context of the reported cohorts, but broader generalizability requires confirmation.” Anatomical studies by Rupp et al. [ 49 ] have identified critical areas of risk during PFO, emphasizing the need for careful surgical technique to avoid damage to the common peroneal nerve and its muscular branches, as well as the anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve. The included studies suggest a potential advantage of PFO regarding earlier weight-bearing and return to basic activities compared to more extensive procedures like TKA. As TKA is more extensive, it usually demands a longer recovery time. Prior literature indicates [ 50 – 52 ] that TKA patients might need weeks or months to regain meaningful function and activity. Post-TKA rehabilitation generally involves physical therapy and a progressive increase in activity levels to ensure proper healing. While direct comparative data on recovery times between PFO and TKA are limited in this analysis, the overall trend implies that PFO might allow patients to recover certain activities more quickly than TKA. However, more research is needed to clearly define these recovery timelines. However, the evidence for this is indirect and based on limited, often non-comparative data within the included studies. A direct, rigorous comparison of recovery trajectories between PFO and established procedures like TKA or HTO is lacking. Therefore, claims regarding superior recovery times with PFO remain preliminary and require robust comparative studies. Currently, there’s a lack of large - scale, high - level comparative trials directly comparing PFO with HTO and TKA in terms of long - term efficacy, complication rates, and functional recovery. A meta - analysis by Wu et al. [ 54 ] indicates that PFO and HTO yield comparable short - term outcomes in KOA treatment. Yet, PFO surpasses HTO in reducing operation time, intraoperative bleeding, hospital stay, and postoperative complications. Some studies [ 55 ] suggest PFO offers early - onset effects, minimal invasiveness, and shorter operation time. But HTO may have better long - term outcomes. More trials are needed in the future to compare the clinical efficacy and safety of PFO with other surgeries. Limitation This systematic review and meta analysis presents a comprehensive evaluation of the clinical and radiological outcomes of PFO in MKOA. While the study includes a large number of patients, several important limitations remain. The majority of included studies are retrospective and observational, with only a few randomized controlled trials, thus limiting the strength of the evidence due to potential bias and uncontrolled confounders. The heterogeneity among studies especially regarding patient selection, follow-up duration, radiological measurements, and perioperative management reduces the reliability and comparability of pooled results. Additionally, radiological outcome data remain underreported in many studies, and long-term efficacy beyond two years is largely unknown. Although the meta-analysis identifies positive short-term effects of PFO, including pain relief and correction of varus deformity, the absence of standardized reporting (consistent use of Kellgren-Lawrence grades, core imaging criteria) weakens the interpretability of findings. Furthermore, the generalizability of the results is limited, as most included studies originate from China and India, with minimal representation of Western or ethnically diverse populations. Finally, the conclusion highlights the need for further high-quality, multicenter, long-term trials to better determine the role of PFO in comparison with established procedures such as HTO and TKA. Conclusion In the treatment of medial compartment knee osteoarthritis (MKOA), proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO) has demonstrated certain potential. This meta-analysis shows that clinical function scores and radiological assessments improved after PFO, indicating that this surgical method can significantly alleviate patients’ symptoms, correct the varus deformity of the lower limb alignment, and is safe. However, it should be noted that the quality of evidence supporting this conclusion is still relatively low, and radiological studies are relatively limited. Therefore, future studies need to be conducted in more diverse patient populations, incorporating more radiological indicators and providing higher-quality clinical evidence. documents.title: Previous knee surgery increases risks of revision, infection, pain and stiffness after knee replacement arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee replacement arthroplasty(KRA), including Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), is the primary method for treating end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, a history of previous knee surgeries (such as knee arthroscopy, ligament reconstruction, meniscectomy, high tibial osteotomy, etc.) may potentially affect functional recovery and complication risks after knee replacement. Although some studies have proposed such associations, the existing evidence remains controversial, and there is a lack of systematic quantitative analysis. This study aims to assess the impact of previous knee surgery on functional outcomes and complications following KRA.
METHODS: Following the PRISMA Guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases up to August 4, 2024, for relevant studies. Demographic data, postoperative complications, and functional changes after primary KRA were evaluated in patients with and without a history of previous knee surgery. Statistical analysis of the included studies was performed using Stata 15.1 software. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to assess the quality of the studies.
RESULTS: This meta-analysis included 28 studies with 703,103 patients (35,535 with a history of previous knee surgery and 667,568 primary KRA patients). Compared to the primary knee surgery group, the previous knee surgery group had significantly higher rates of prosthetic aseptic revision (RR(95%CI) = 1.45 (1.18-1.78)) (relative risk, RR; Confidence Interval, CI), infection (RR(95%CI) = 1.36 (1.11-1.67)), knee stiffness (RR(95%CI) = 1.73 (1.02-2.96)), and knee pain (RR(95%CI) = 1.21 (1.08-1.34)). However, there were no significant differences in changes in Knee Society Score (KSS) function (WMD(95%CI) = -0.51 (-1.73 to 0.72)) (weighted mean difference, WMD), KSS pain score (WMD(95%CI) = 0.41 (-2.97 to 3.79)), or other knee function scores.
CONCLUSION: Patients with a history of previous knee surgery have a higher likelihood of prosthetic revision, a greater risk of surgical site infections or periprosthetic infections, and a significantly higher incidence of knee stiffness and knee pain following KRA.

Abstract Background Knee replacement arthroplasty(KRA), including Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), is the primary method for treating end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, a history of previous knee surgeries (such as knee arthroscopy, ligament reconstruction, meniscectomy, high tibial osteotomy, etc.) may potentially affect functional recovery and complication risks after knee replacement. Although some studies have proposed such associations, the existing evidence remains controversial, and there is a lack of systematic quantitative analysis. This study aims to assess the impact of previous knee surgery on functional outcomes and complications following KRA. Methods Following the PRISMA Guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases up to August 4, 2024, for relevant studies. Demographic data, postoperative complications, and functional changes after primary KRA were evaluated in patients with and without a history of previous knee surgery. Statistical analysis of the included studies was performed using Stata 15.1 software. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to assess the quality of the studies. Results This meta-analysis included 28 studies with 703,103 patients (35,535 with a history of previous knee surgery and 667,568 primary KRA patients). Compared to the primary knee surgery group, the previous knee surgery group had significantly higher rates of prosthetic aseptic revision (RR(95%CI) = 1.45 (1.18–1.78)) (relative risk, RR; Confidence Interval, CI), infection (RR(95%CI) = 1.36 (1.11–1.67)), knee stiffness (RR(95%CI) = 1.73 (1.02–2.96)), and knee pain (RR(95%CI) = 1.21 (1.08–1.34)). However, there were no significant differences in changes in Knee Society Score (KSS) function (WMD(95%CI) = -0.51 (-1.73 to 0.72)) (weighted mean difference, WMD), KSS pain score (WMD(95%CI) = 0.41 (-2.97 to 3.79)), or other knee function scores. Conclusion Patients with a history of previous knee surgery have a higher likelihood of prosthetic revision, a greater risk of surgical site infections or periprosthetic infections, and a significantly higher incidence of knee stiffness and knee pain following KRA. Introduction Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a chronic degenerative joint disease caused by various factors (such as obesity, gender, genetics, joint injuries, etc.), leading to the degeneration, erosion, and destruction of articular cartilage, as well as bone spur formation at the joint margins, resulting in clinical symptoms like pain, swelling, deformity, and functional impairment. Its incidence rate is extremely high [ 1 , 2 ]. From 1990 to 2019, the global prevalence of KOA increased by 48%, accounting for 2% of the global disease burden and ranking as the 15th leading cause of disability worldwide, with years lived with disability (YLD) being particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries [ 3 ]. By 2020, the total global population with KOA reached 654 million, with a prevalence of 19.2% in Europe and 13.4% in Asia. That year alone, there were 86.7 million new cases [ 4 , 5 ]. As global aging continues and the incidence of KOA rises, the number of patients requiring knee replacement surgery is expected to significantly increase in the future. As an important treatment method for KOA, Knee replacement arthroplasty (KRA) represents the final step in a stepwise treatment approach, providing support for other treatment options [ 2 , 6 ]. However, KRA is complex, and the patient’s postoperative recovery directly affects treatment outcomes and complication rates. For some knee replacement surgery patients, the same knee joint has previously undergone other surgeries, which has become an important issue in clinical practice. Some studies suggest that, compared to patients who have never had knee surgery, a history of previous knee surgeries may adversely affect functional recovery after knee replacement surgery and increase the risk of complications (such as infection rates, aseptic loosening of prosthetics, etc.) [ 7 – 12 ]. Moreover, some studies have shown that patients with a history of knee surgery experience more pronounced postoperative pain and stiffness, with a relatively poorer improvement in knee joint range of motion [ 13 ]. Although multiple studies have explored the effects of previous knee surgeries on the outcomes of knee replacement surgery, there is inconsistency between the existing studies. Some studies have found that a history of knee surgery does not significantly affect joint function or complications after knee replacement surgery [ 14 ], and some even suggest that certain postoperative indicators in the study group are better than those in the control group [ 15 – 18 ]. Currently, there are no unified clinical guidelines or expert consensus clearly stating whether a history of previous knee surgeries significantly impacts the prognosis of knee replacement surgery. Current meta-analyses on the impact of prior knee surgery on knee replacement outcomes remain limited, and existing studies predominantly focus on singular types of prior surgeries and knee replacement procedures, lacking comprehensive evaluation. This study aims to explore the impact of a history of previous knee surgeries on postoperative function and complications after knee replacement surgery, providing valuable references for clinical practice and preoperative risk assessment for patients. Materials and methods This study was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P 2015 statement) guidelines [ 19 ]. The study protocol has been published on PROSPERO (CRD42025611219). Ethical approval and patient informed consent were not required for this study. Search process This electronic search was independently performed by two researchers (LYL and WZN) in databases including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science, with the search period from the establishment of the database to August 4, 2024. The search strategy was adapted for each database and was based on the MeSH terms “Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee; Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction; Arthroscopy; Meniscectomy; Synovectomy” and their free-text terms to construct the search query. Boolean operators “OR” and “AND” were used to combine the terms. Additionally, we reviewed the reference lists of the studies identified during the search to find other relevant studies. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The titles and abstracts of all initially identified studies were independently reviewed. Studies that met the following inclusion criteria were included in this review: (i) The study design was a cohort study or case-control study; (ii) The language of the study was English; (iii) The study subjects were clinically diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis and met the surgical indications for knee replacement, with the study group having a history of knee surgery and the control group having no history of knee surgery; (iv)This is about primary KRA, both the study and control groups received knee replacement surgery using the same surgical method; (v)The minimum number of cases included in the study was 20, and the minimum follow-up time was 3 months.Exclusion criteria included: (i) Reviews, letters, expert opinions, editorials, non-controlled studies, other technical comparisons, meta-analyses, case reports, conference papers, animal studies, cadaveric studies, guidelines, and short surveys; (ii) Studies for which the full text could not be accessed; (iii) Studies with non-research subjects, non-English literature, improper or missing controls, or improper or missing interventions. Literature screening and data extraction The inclusion and exclusion criteria were strictly followed to screen the literature. Endnote X9 software was used to manage all the retrieved studies. After importing the studies into Endnote X9 and removing duplicates, studies were initially selected based on titles or abstracts. Full-text articles were downloaded, and after reading the full texts, studies that met the criteria for this systematic review were included. Basic information from the selected studies was extracted and cross-checked for consistency, and measurement units were standardized. If there were discrepancies, a third researcher (HQ) was consulted to make the final decision. After thorough discussion, the research team concluded that since knee fractures—whether surgically treated or not—may inevitably lead to Post-Traumatic Osteoarthritis (PTOA) and subsequently affect TKA outcomes, patients with knee fractures were excluded from the study. The extracted information mainly included the title, first author, publication year, country, sample size, gender, patient age, history of prior surgery, follow-up period, and outcome measures. Assessment of study quality Researchers independently use the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) to assess the quality of the selected studies. In case of disagreement, a third researcher was consulted to Make a judgment, resolve the discrepancy, and reach a consensus. For cohort studies, the assessment included the following 8 aspects: (i) Representativeness of the exposed cohort; (ii) Selection of the non-exposed cohort; (iii) Definition of exposure; (iv) No outcome events occurred in the cohort prior to the study; (v) Comparability of cohorts based on design or analysis; (vi) Outcome assessment; (vii) Adequacy of follow-up to observe the occurrence of outcomes; (viii) Completeness of follow-up. For case-control studies, the assessment included the following 8 aspects: (i) Adequacy of case definition; (ii) Representativeness of the cases; (iii) Selection of controls; (iv) Definition of controls; (v) Comparability of cases and controls based on design or analysis; (vi) Definition of exposure; (vii) Whether the same method was used for determining exposure in both cases and controls; (viii) Non-response rate. Scores of 1–3 points were classified as low quality, 4–6 points as moderate quality, and 7–9 points as high quality. Outcome measures The primary outcome measures: (i) Prosthesis revision rate; (ii) Periprosthetic joint infection(PJI) rate. The secondary outcome measures: (i) Knee Society Score functional score (KSS functional score); (ii) Knee Society Score pain score (KSS pain score); (iii) Incidence of stiffness; (iv) Range of motion (ROM) of the knee joint; (v) Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS); (vi) Oxford Knee Score (OKS); (vii) Manipulation under anesthesia rate (MUA); (viii) International Knee Society Score functional score (IKS functional score); (ix) International Knee Society Score clinical score (IKS clinical score); (x) Pain incidence. Data on secondary outcomes are presented in the Supplementary Material. Statistical analysis The extracted data were entered into Stata 15.1 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX, USA) for statistical analysis. For binary variable data such as prosthesis revision rate, prosthesis infection rate, incidence of stiffness, incidence of pain, and manipulation under anesthesia rate (MUA), event counts were used, and relative risk (RR) was applied as the effect size. For continuous data such as KSS functional/pain scores, KOOS, OKS, IKS functional/clinical scores, and knee joint range of motion, the data were recorded as mean and standard deviation, and weighted mean difference(WMD) was used as the effect size. Both effect sizes were reported with a 95% confidence interval (CI). The heterogeneity of the included studies was assessed using the Chi-square test and the inconsistency index (I²). If I² < 50%, it indicates no significant heterogeneity between studies, and a fixed-effect model was used for analysis. If I² > 50%, it indicates significant heterogeneity, and a random-effects model was used for analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed based on the type of knee replacement and previous surgery to explore the sources of heterogeneity, followed by sensitivity analyses. To assess publication bias, we used Egger’s test and visually examined the funnel plot. A P value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Literature search results A total of 13,326 articles were retrieved, including 1,812 from PubMed, 5,550 from Web of Science, 5,509 from Embase, and 455 from The Cochrane Library. After excluding duplicate articles, 10,214 articles remained, and 70 articles underwent full-text review. Based on the inclusion criteria, after full-text screening, 28 articles were ultimately included in the study [ 7 – 18 , 20 – 35 ]. The literature search flow and results were shown in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Study selection process Basic characteristics of the included studies There were 28 studies included, comprising 703,103 patients diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis who required knee replacement surgery (surgery types included TKA/UKA). Among these, the study group included 35,535 patients with a history of knee surgery, which comprised: Knee soft tissue surgeries (including knee arthroscopy (KA), anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (PCLR), multi-ligament knee injury surgeries (MLKI), etc.); Knee bone surgeries (mainly high tibial osteotomy (HTO)); Unknown knee surgery types (studies that did not specify the specific knee surgery type). The control group comprised 667,568 patients, with no history of invasive procedures or infections on the same side knee. Both the study and control groups had no history of knee infections. Sensitivity analysis A sensitivity analysis was performed by individually excluding each study from the meta-analysis to assess whether the results were overly influenced by a single study. The results of the sensitivity analysis showed that all the meta-analysis results were stable and reliable. Publication bias We conducted a publication bias analysis for all the included outcomes. Funnel plots were visually examined for publication bias, and Egger’s test was used to analyze the funnel plots. A P -value > 0.05 was considered to indicate no publication bias. The results revealed that there was no publication bias for any of the merged outcome measures, and the results were robust and reliable. Subgroup analysis The types of surgeries for the patients included TKA and UKA, which may have different postoperative outcomes. The prior surgical history includes soft tissue knee surgeries (such as Knee arthroscopy(KA), Anterior Cruciate Ligament Rupture (ACLR), Posterior Cruciate Ligament Rupture (PCLR), Multiple Ligament Knee Injuries (MLKI) surgeries, etc.), bone surgeries (such as High Tibial Osteotomy(HTO)), and unknown previous surgical types. The postoperative outcomes might vary according to different prior surgical histories. To investigate the impact of different knee replacement surgery types and prior surgical histories on complications and function after knee replacement, subgroup analysis of various study indicators was conducted based on the existing outcome measures and the main outcome indicators were displayed. Subgroup analysis of prosthetic revision rate We conducted a subgroup analysis based on different previous surgical types to study their impact on the prosthetic revision rate after knee replacement surgery. The knee soft tissue surgery group included 22 studies for analysis, with high heterogeneity between studies (I²=76.1%, P < 0.001). In the study group compared to the control group, the prosthetic revision rate was significantly higher, and the result was statistically significant (RR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.08–1.92). The knee bone surgery group included 2 studies for analysis, with low heterogeneity between studies (I²=0.0%, P = 0.847). In the study group compared to the control group, the prosthetic revision rate was significantly higher, and the result was statistically significant (RR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.10–1.63). The unknown surgical type group (without categorizing all knee surgeries) included 2 studies for analysis, with high heterogeneity between studies (I²=79.7%, P = 0.026). In the study group compared to the control group, the prosthetic revision rate was significantly higher, and the result was statistically significant (RR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.06–2.43). We conducted a subgroup analysis based on different types of knee replacement surgeries. The TKA group included 22 studies for analysis, with high heterogeneity between studies (I²=76.10%, P < 0.001). In the study group compared to the control group, the prosthetic revision rate was significantly higher, and the result was statistically significant (RR = 1.46, 95% CI: 1.17–1.83). The UKA group included 4 studies for analysis, with moderate heterogeneity between studies (I²=54.8%, P = 0.085). In the study group compared to the control group, the prosthetic revision rate was slightly higher, but the difference was not statistically significant (RR = 1.30, 95% CI: 0.63–2.68) (Table 3 ).
